title: Cost economics pilot discussion - Kestrel Software
summary: Intro call to scope a small pilot to validate per-token economics and tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Kestrel wants to understand realistic per-inference cost for their chat assistant (avg seq lengths, concurrency), what levers (batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization) move the needle, and what committed capacity would look like for Dedicated. Action: Redwood to send a cost-model spreadsheet, SOC2/security pack, and propose a 2-week pilot plan with benchmark steps.
next_steps: Alex to send cost model spreadsheet and example invoices (by 2025-03-20)
Priya to propose pilot benchmark plan and test scripts (by 2025-03-21)
Martin to provide representative prompt set and traffic profile (by 2025-03-21)
Schedule a Dedicated sizing call if pilot numbers look good (tentative 2025-03-26)
action_items: Alex - Send cost model spreadsheet and pricing note - due 2025-03-20
Priya - Draft 2-week pilot benchmark plan with test harness and perf targets - due 2025-03-21
Martin - Share 3 sample prompt sets and 7-day traffic histogram - due 2025-03-21
Omar - Confirm network/VPC restrictions and KMS vendor - due 2025-03-22
questions: Can Redwood meet sub-200ms 95p latency for 512-token responses?
How much does batching impact tail latency for interactive chat?
What is the expected delta (per-token) between Hosted and Dedicated?
Does Redwood support customer-managed KMS in Private?
transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2025-03-18 15:30 UTC. Duration: ~57 minutes. Recording: auto. Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Martin Reyes (Kestrel CTO), Jasmine Patel (Kestrel ML Eng), Omar Alvi (Infra).

[00:00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick round of intros and then we'll jump into the cost/pricing stuff Martin sent over.
[00:00:08] Martin Reyes: Yep, thanks Alex. On our side I'm Martin, CTO, Jasmine is ML, Omar is infra. We're looking to run a pilot to figure out unit economics for our assistant — cost per "use" basically.
[00:00:18] Priya Desai: Awesome. To set expectations: we usually map per-token pricing to per-turn cost given your avg prompt/response lengths, and then show levers — batching, prefix/KV caching, quant — that typically reduce unit spend.
[00:00:28] Jasmine Patel: Quick note: our current assistant average prompt is ~120 tokens in, ~280 tokens out. Peak concurrency is around 80 rps during spikes, but steady is more like 10-15 rps.
[00:00:37] Omar Alvi: Security is a must - we need SOC2, SAML SSO, and customer-managed KMS if we go private. Also network egress rules may force an on-prem connector for some sensitive workloads.
[00:00:47] Alex Chen: Totally. We'll include SOC2 pack and KMS options in the follow-up. For the cost math — do you have a target budget or target cost per active user?
[00:00:55] Martin Reyes: We're trying to keep inference to < $0.015 per end-user per day initially; with ~10k active DAUs that caps us at about $1500/day. But that's rough. We mostly want to know what affects that number.
[00:01:05] Priya Desai: Good anchor. If we translate that to tokens, with your avg sizes — say 400 tokens per turn — that gives you roughly 3.75k turns per day at that budget. We can walk through three deployment options: Hosted (pay-per-use), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and Private (VPC/on-prem with platform fee).

[00:05:10] [topic shift] Pricing mechanics and examples
[00:05:12] Alex Chen: For Hosted, our published per-token rates vary by model family; for example, a 13B open model used for chat might be $0.0006 per 1k input tokens and $0.0012 per 1k output tokens — rough numbers. For Dedicated, you get a committed capacity price — effectively a fixed monthly fee for a pool and then much lower variable cost per token, because the amortized infra is known.
[00:05:40] Jasmine Patel: Can you quantify 'much lower'? Like percent delta?
[00:05:45] Priya Desai: In our experience, Dedicated can reduce your unit infrastructure cost 40-70% compared to pure Hosted at scale, depending a lot on utilization, batching efficiency, and sequence length distribution. If you get >60% utilization and good batching, the per-token infra cost drops significantly. But there's a capex-like commitment.
[00:06:10] Martin Reyes: So if we commit to a Dedicated pool, what's the minimum? We aren't huge yet.
[00:06:16] Alex Chen: We offer smaller reserved tiers for pilots — not full enterprise-only. For example, a half-pod equivalent reserved rack for 3 months is an option; we'll include exact numbers in the spreadsheet. The key trade is throughput predictability vs per-token elasticity.
[00:06:32] Omar Alvi: Any hard SLO numbers? We need 99.9% availability and sub-250ms p95 for short chats ideally.
[00:06:40] Priya Desai: Availability wise Dedicated can meet an SLA. Latency is trickier — p95 of 250ms for 512-token responses is aggressive unless you use a trimmed model or aggressive batching configs. For short responses (<=128 tokens) p95 <200ms is realistic on well-packed GPUs. We'll need to run benchmarks against your actual prompt mix.

[00:10:05] [topic shift] Batching and caching levers
[00:10:07] Jasmine Patel: Walk me through batching — does batching always save money? How does it affect tail latency?
[00:10:12] Priya Desai: Batching reduces per-token compute overhead by combining multiple in-flight requests; effective batch size and sequence-length variance are the main factors. For throughput workloads, batching gives large savings. For interactive chat with strict latency SLOs, you tune a batching policy (max wait ms, max batch size). That reduces cost but can slightly increase p95.
[00:10:36] Alex Chen: We also offer prefix/KV cache where repeated context (like system prompt and user profile) is cached — for multi-turn flows that reuse context, that can cut compute by 20-60% depending on how much of the token stream is cached.
[00:10:49] Martin Reyes: Our assistant reuses a lot of system prompt and user persona data; could be high hit-rate. How are cache hits measured?
[00:10:55] Priya Desai: Cache hit rates are measured at request time in the console per key. We'll surface token-savings and estimated dollar-savings in the cost-model spreadsheet. Also, KV cache helps latency because the model doesn't need to recompute from scratch — so it's a double win if your flows are cache-friendly.

[00:13:20] [timestamped snippet]
[00:13:22] Jasmine Patel: What about quantization? We heard 4-bit quant yields big memory savings.
[00:13:25] Priya Desai: Yes, quantization (4-bit/8-bit) drops memory and can allow larger batch sizes per GPU which reduces cost per token. There's a small quality delta; we can run evals on your prompt sets to quantify. For retrieval-augmented tasks it's often indistinguishable in quality.
[00:13:42] Martin Reyes: If we run quantized models in Dedicated, does that change licensing or support?
[00:13:47] Alex Chen: No license delta. We qualify and verify model variants. We'll note any model-specific caveats in the onboarding doc.

[00:17:00] [topic shift] Example cost calc walk-through
[00:17:02] Priya Desai: Let's do a toy calc: 10k DAU, 1.2 turns per DAU per day average = 12k turns/day. With 400 tokens/turn that's 4.8M tokens/day. On Hosted if we assume $0.0012 per 1k output tokens and $0.0006 per 1k input tokens -> rough daily infra cost: inputs 4.8M*0.0006/1000 = $2.88, outputs 4.8M*0.0012/1000 = $5.76 -> total ~$8.64/day. That seems low because those example per-k rates are for small open models; real rates for larger models are higher.
[00:17:34] Jasmine Patel: Wait those sample rates seem off; our current invoices with another vendor are like $2000/month for a similar volume.
[00:17:41] Alex Chen: Right — the numbers depend on model size and provider. The example was to show calc mechanics. For a production-grade 34B or so model, you should expect higher per-token numbers; and Hosted also includes platform overhead. We'll put realistic model examples in the spreadsheet (13B, 34B, quantized 34B) and map to your traffic.

[00:21:10] [background noise/crosstalk briefly]
[00:21:14] Omar Alvi: From infra side, if we go Dedicated, what control do we have over instance placement, region, VPC peering? We have some data residency constraints in EU.
[00:21:23] Priya Desai: Dedicated can be provisioned in region-specific clusters; Private gives you a customer-controlled VPC. Dedicated also supports VPC peering for secure egress. For the pilot we'd recommend Hosted in the same region to run initial benchmarks, and then move to Dedicated or Private once numbers validate.

[00:25:00] [topic: pilot scope]
[00:25:02] Alex Chen: Proposed pilot: 2 weeks, run a benchmark harness with your prompt set, simulate production concurrency profile, measure p50/p95 latency, batch-hit rates, KV cache hit rates, and cost per 1k tokens. We'll run it against three model configs: 13B (float16), 34B (float16), and 34B (4-bit quant).
[00:25:18] Jasmine Patel: Sounds good. What do you need from us?
[00:25:20] Priya Desai: 1) prompt set (representative), 2) traffic histogram (minute-level for peak), 3) success metrics — what is acceptable latency and cost target. Also network details for Private tests.

[00:29:44] [noise]
[00:29:47] Martin Reyes: On success metrics: we need p95 <= 300ms for 256-token responses and 400ms for 512-token responses, ideally. Budget target is $0.015 per active user per day as I said. If you show a path to that with Dedicated plus caching that's ideal.
[00:30:05] Alex Chen: We'll model that. One nuance: p95 includes queuing introduced by batching. For the pilot we'll run different batching policies (aggressive batch to maximize throughput vs latency-optimized minimal wait) and produce cost/latency tradeoff curves.

[00:33:10] [topic: security/compliance briefly]
[00:33:12] Omar Alvi: Quick question: for Private, can we keep keys in AWS KMS/HSM? We need customer-managed keys.
[00:33:18] Alex Chen: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS and on-prem HSM integrations. We'll include integration notes and SOC2 docs in the follow-up packet.

[00:36:55] [topic: pricing and billing cadence]
[00:36:58] Jasmine Patel: How does billing look for Dedicated? Monthly invoice? Commit terms?
[00:37:03] Alex Chen: Typically monthly for reserved capacity with contract terms; Dedicated has a base committed fee and then variable egress and overage charges if you exceed reserved throughput. For pilots we often do short-term reserved credits to emulate Dedicated without long-term lock.
[00:37:18] Martin Reyes: If our usage is bursty, do you have burst/buffer capacity?
[00:37:22] Priya Desai: Yes, burst buckets and autoscale policies are configurable; you can pay a premium for guaranteed burst or use fallback routing to Hosted for spikes. We'll explore cost implications in the spreadsheet.

[00:41:00] [topic: competitor call-outs]
[00:41:02] Martin Reyes: We've talked to vendor X and Y — they offered lower base Hosted rates but limited observability. Monitoring and token-level cost breakdown is important to us.
[00:41:12] Alex Chen: We can export token-level traces and per-route dashboards. That was one of our differentiators. We'll include sample console screenshots.

[00:45:30] [recap]
[00:45:32] Alex Chen: Quick recap: Redwood will send cost-model with real model examples, propose the 2-week pilot benchmark plan, include SOC2/KMS docs, and propose Dedicated half-pod pilot pricing. Kestrel will send prompt sets and traffic histogram. Next meeting to review pilot plan and sign pilot SOW.
[00:45:50] Martin Reyes: Sounds good. One more ask: can you include examples of real invoices or customer cost decks (anonymized) so we can sanity-check?
[00:45:58] Alex Chen: Yes, we'll anonymize and send example invoices.

[00:50:00] [closing]
[00:50:02] Jasmine Patel: Thanks all, excited to see the spreadsheet.
[00:50:05] Omar Alvi: Thanks. We'll get the prompt sets over tomorrow.
[00:50:10] Priya Desai: Great, we'll kick off the pilot plan and loop in support.
[00:50:15] Alex Chen: Appreciate it — end call.

Notes on transcription: automated transcript had occasional mislabels (e.g., "Priya" sometimes 'Speaker 2'), and a couple of acronyms mangled (KMS -> K-M-S or sometimes KMS). There was brief background noise around 00:21 and 00:29 where a line from Martin clipped.
